summary: Jesus comforts His troubled disciples: He goes to prepare a place for them, He is the way to the Father, and He promises the Helper and His peace.
key_insight: “Let not your heart be troubled” was spoken on the night Jesus’ own spirit was troubled; John uses the same word for Him (12:27; 13:21). He said it to men who had just heard that one of them would betray Him and Peter would deny Him. His comfort does not deny the trouble; it gives them Himself in the middle of it.
story: “Let not your heart be troubled; you believe in God, believe also in Me.” In His Father’s house were many mansions, and He was going to prepare a place for them. “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to Myself; that where I am, there you may be also.” They knew where He was going, He said, and they knew the way.

Thomas said, “Lord, we do not know where You are going, and how can we know the way?” Jesus answered, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” If they had known Him, they would have known His Father also; from now on they knew Him and had seen Him.

Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is sufficient for us.” Jesus said, “Have I been with you so long, and yet you have not known Me, Philip? He who has seen Me has seen the Father.” He was in the Father and the Father in Him; His words and works were the Father’s. Whoever believed in Him would do the works He did, and greater works, because He was going to the Father. Whatever they asked in His name, He would do.

“If you love Me, keep My commandments.” He would pray the Father, and the Father would give them another Helper to be with them forever, the Spirit of truth. The world could not receive Him, but they knew Him, “for He dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” In a little while the world would see Him no more, but they would see Him. “Because I live, you will live also.”

Judas (not Iscariot) asked how He would show Himself to them and not to the world. Jesus answered, “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word; and My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.” The Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send in His name, would teach them all things and remind them of everything He had said.

“Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.” If they loved Him, they would rejoice that He was going to the Father, for the Father was greater than He. He would not talk with them much longer, “for the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in Me.” But He would do as the Father commanded, so that the world might know He loved the Father. “Arise, let us go from here.”

scene.label: My Father’s house
scene.text: Jesus had called the temple “My Father’s house” when He drove out the sellers (John 2:16). Now He uses the phrase for the Father’s own dwelling. The word translated “mansions” means dwelling places or rooms; the picture is a place in the family home, not a separate estate.

scene.label: Thomas and Philip
scene.text: John gives both men a voice more than once. Thomas had said, “Let us also go, that we may die with Him” (11:16); Philip had counted the cost of bread for the five thousand (6:7). Both speak plainly, and their honest questions draw out two of Jesus’ clearest statements about Himself.

scene.label: Judas (not Iscariot)
scene.text: Luke calls him “Judas the son of James” (Luke 6:16); he is probably the Thaddaeus named by Matthew and Mark. John adds “not Iscariot” to keep the two apart, since the betrayer had just left the room.

scene.label: Peace
scene.text: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday Jewish greeting and farewell. Jesus turns the ordinary word into a parting gift: His own peace, the wholeness the prophets promised with the Messiah, the “Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

witnesses.john: Only John records this farewell. Spoken after Judas left, it turns the disciples from the shock of betrayal and denial to the Father’s house, the way through Jesus, and the coming of the Spirit. Its center, “He who has seen Me has seen the Father,” states plainly what John wrote at the start: the Son has made the Father known (1:18).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is not one guide among many but the way itself, and the One in whom the Father is seen. He speaks as the Son going home to His Father, who will come again for His own and meanwhile send the Spirit to live in them.
seeing.living: Thomas did not know the way, and Philip wanted to see the Father; Jesus answered both by pointing to Himself. When your heart is troubled about what lies ahead, look at Jesus and trust His word that He has prepared a place and will come for you. His peace is given, not earned, and it does not depend on how the world treats you.
seeing.ponder: If whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father, what does that tell you about the God you pray to?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus calms troubled hearts by showing them the Father in Himself.
outline: The Father seen in the Son (8–14)
preaching.watch_for: The word translated “mansions” in verse 2 is the same Greek word Jesus uses in verse 23, where the Father and the Son “make Our home” with whoever loves Him. Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for His people with the Father; meanwhile, the Father and the Son come to dwell with them.
